item.description:

item.title: High-speed train crash in Spain kills at least 68, dozens injured
item.description:
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped in central Spain, derailing two cars and killing at least 68 people Wednesday morning, according to local authorities.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers continue searching the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, according to Spain's rail system operator ADIF. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Emergency services attend to the victims at the scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026.
Juanma Jiménez/AP
Padilla told state broadcaster TVE the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.
The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January. Padilla said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers were in the IRYO train.
"Today all of Spain is grieving," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.

item.title: Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil, lands in U.S. after election loss
item.description:
Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and his family left the country on Tuesday after he lost Brazil's hotly contested presidential election over the weekend, and landed in Miami Wednesday morning.
Earlier, a senior State Department official told CBS News that Bolsonaro and his family would receive U.S. visas.
Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump, departed Brazil for the U.S. days after being defeated by incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election. En route to the U.S., Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters first arrived in Argentina and then took a private plane to Guayaquil, Ecuador, according to Argentinian officials and flight tracking data.
In a letter to the Brazilian people posted on X, Bolsonaro called the election results illegitimate and accused the government of targeting him for persecution.
"Facing the political weaponization of Justice in Brazil, I decided to move with my family to the United States, where we are safe. I personally thank President Trump and the American government for welcoming us," he said in the letter, translated from the Portuguese. He added, "I want to make it clear: I did not flee Brazil; I left for the sake of Brazil."
Silva said Tuesday it was "shameful" that Bolsonaro had fled Brazil.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," Silva said, per Agence France-Presse. "The act of leaving Brazil is shameful."
Bolsonaro's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election.
Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with Mr. Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: Brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.

item.title: Russell Brand takes the stand at his rape and sexual assault trial
item.description:
Actor and comedian Russell Brand took the stand in his trial on rape and sexual assault charges in London on Wednesday.
Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. Brand has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
He started the morning by answering questions on whether he committed each respective charge with a terse "no." Under cross-examination, he said he was innocent.
"My entire life has been consumed by these allegations," Brand said in his initial questioning. Under cross-examination, he said that while he believes he behaved promiscuously during the time period in question, he thinks that "consent is absolutely non-negotiable."
Russell Brand and wife Laura Brand arrive at court ahead of his trial, at Southwark Crown Court on October 28, 2026.
Alberto Pezzali / Getty Images
Brand calls consent "more important than sex itself"
One woman alleged she met Brand at a Labour Party conference in 1999. She believed Brand was gay, and invited him to her hotel room to continue a conversation that began after a cabaret show where he performed. She alleged he came out of the bathroom topless before raping her.
Brand said he remembers meeting the victim and chatting with her. When asked if he portrayed himself as gay, he said, "I don't think so." Brand said the victim was the one who suggested returning to her hotel room.
Brand said he believes he would have checked in with the woman during the encounter, and denied raping her. He said he believes "consent is fundamental, essential, necessary, and in many ways, more important than sex itself."

item.title: No clear winner in Israeli election as polls suggest stalemate
item.description:
No clear winner emerged in Israel's elections on Wednesday with the vote count still under way. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition nor the opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, secured a majority, according to exit polls on Tuesday night.
With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%, according to official election data.
Local media projected 53 seats for Likud and allied parties, 48 for Yashar and allied parties and 19 for Arab-led parties. Each would need 61 seats for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
On Wednesday morning, the head of Israel's main left-wing party called for his opposition allies to work with Arab parties to unseat Netanyahu.
"We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," Yair Golan said on X. "We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens."
Netanyahu dismissed the idea of partnership with Arab parties, instead calling on his allies to form a "right-wing, nationalist government."
"We must not endanger Israel and establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties," Netanyahu said on Wednesday morning.
Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.
Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have previously vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.
